job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

passage: India experiences a highly uneven distribution of rainfall, with regions like Mawsynram receiving over 11,000 mm annually, while parts of Rajasthan receive less than 200 mm. Despite this, many believe that rain will naturally refill all our resources, ignoring that only a fraction of rainfall infiltrates the soil to recharge aquifers. Groundwater is a finite treasure, yet many think a dry borewell simply requires deeper drilling, failing to realize that the water table is dropping globally due to over-extraction. Furthermore, our water footprint extends far beyond the tap; producing a single kilogram of rice requires approximately 2,500 litres of water, far more than the few litres used for daily bathing. We often dismiss greywater from washing clothes as useless waste, yet this water can be safely treated and reused for gardening or flushing. Similarly, drip irrigation is often misunderstood as less effective than flooding, even though it delivers water directly to the roots, significantly reducing evaporation losses. Every individual, regardless of age, must recognize that usable freshwater is a limited resource. By adopting rainwater harvesting to recharge groundwater and fixing minor leaks that waste thousands of litres annually, we can secure our future. Saving water is not just a government responsibility; it is a vital daily habit for every student.

items.evidence: India experiences a highly uneven distribution of rainfall, with regions like Mawsynram receiving over 11,000 mm annually, while parts of Rajasthan receive less than 200 mm.
items.q: Why might a school in Rajasthan need to save water more than one in Mawsynram?
options: It gets far less rain every year
It gets the same rain as all of India
It gets over 11,000 mm of rain yearly
It gets more rain, but floods waste it
items.explain: Rain in India is uneven: Rajasthan gets under 200 mm, while Mawsynram gets over 11,000 mm.

wrong.why: thinks every part of India gets similar rain
reverses which place gets more rain

items.evidence: Despite this, many believe that rain will naturally refill all our resources, ignoring that only a fraction of rainfall infiltrates the soil to recharge aquifers.
items.q: Heavy rain falls on a town. Will all of it refill the town's aquifers?
options: No, only a small part soaks into soil
Yes, rain naturally refills all our water
Yes, all of it becomes drinking water
No, rain only refills rivers and lakes
items.explain: Only a fraction of rainfall soaks into the soil to recharge aquifers, so rain cannot refill everything.

wrong.why: thinks rain refills all our water
thinks all rain becomes drinking water
thinks rivers and lakes hold most fresh water

items.evidence: Groundwater is a finite treasure, yet many think a dry borewell simply requires deeper drilling, failing to realize that the water table is dropping globally due to over-extraction.
items.q: A family's borewell has dried up. What is the real cause behind it?
options: Overuse is lowering the water table everywhere
This borewell just needs drilling a bit deeper
All water below this area is now gone
It will refill as fast as it was pumped
items.explain: The water table is dropping globally because we pump out too much groundwater, so deeper drilling is no fix.

wrong.why: holds the belief the passage says is mistaken
thinks a dry borewell means no water anywhere below
thinks groundwater refills as fast as it is pumped

items.evidence: Furthermore, our water footprint extends far beyond the tap; producing a single kilogram of rice requires approximately 2,500 litres of water, far more than the few litres used for daily bathing.
items.q: How does the water needed for one kilogram of rice compare with daily bathing?
options: Rice needs far more, about 2,500 litres
Rice needs only a few litres, like bathing
Bathing needs more, since we use it directly
Rice needs about 200 litres, a little more
items.explain: Producing 1 kg of rice needs about 2,500 litres, far more than the few litres used for bathing.

wrong.why: thinks growing rice uses only a few litres
thinks footprint is only water used at the tap
grabs a different number from the passage

items.evidence: Similarly, drip irrigation is often misunderstood as less effective than flooding, even though it delivers water directly to the roots, significantly reducing evaporation losses.
items.q: How does drip irrigation save more water than flooding a field?
options: It sends water straight to roots, cutting evaporation
It uses greywater, so no fresh water is needed
It catches rain, so it refills the groundwater
It floods the soil, so the ground stores more
items.explain: Drip irrigation gives water directly to the roots, so much less is lost to evaporation.

wrong.why: mixes it up with reusing greywater
mixes it up with rainwater harvesting
believes flooding is the better method
